sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Virtualization allows multiple virtual machines and networks to operate on physical infrastructure.
CompTIA wants you to recognize how virtual machines can operate independently, work together, be copied, interact with hardware, use virtual networking, and access different storage systems.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Is the scenario about virtual machine availability, placement, duplication, hardware access, networking, or storage?
sections.callout: What does the virtual machine need from the virtualization environment?

sections.title: Stand-Alone
paragraphs: A stand-alone virtualization host operates independently.
Its virtual machines depend primarily on that host instead of participating in a larger cluster.
Think: One virtualization host doing its own thing.
sections.callout: If a virtualization server works independently without clustered hosts → think stand-alone.

sections.title: Clustering
paragraphs: A virtualization cluster groups multiple hosts together so they can work as a larger system.
Clustering can improve resource availability and workload flexibility.
If one host has a problem, clustered designs may allow workloads to continue or move elsewhere depending on the implementation.
Think: Multiple hosts working as a team.
sections.callout: If several virtualization hosts cooperate for resilience or workload placement → think clustering.

sections.title: Cloning
paragraphs: Cloning creates a copy of an existing virtual machine.
Instead of building another machine manually from the beginning, an existing system can be duplicated.
Think: Copy the virtual machine.
sections.callout: If an identical or similar virtual machine needs to be created quickly from an existing one → think cloning.

sections.title: Host Affinity
paragraphs: Host affinity controls or influences where a virtual machine workload should run.
An organization may want a particular virtual machine to remain on or near a particular virtualization host.
Think: This virtual machine prefers this host.
sections.callout: If the requirement specifies that a virtual machine should run on a particular host → think host affinity.

sections.title: Hardware Pass-Through
paragraphs: Normally, virtualized hardware sits between a virtual machine and the physical device.
Hardware pass-through allows a virtual machine more direct access to specific physical hardware.
This can be useful when the workload needs capabilities of that device directly.
Think: Let the virtual machine talk directly to the real hardware.
sections.callout: If a virtual machine needs direct access to a physical device → think hardware pass-through.

entries.title: Overlay Networks
paragraphs: An overlay network creates a virtual network on top of another underlying network.
The physical network provides connectivity underneath, while the overlay creates logical connections between virtualized resources.
Think: A virtual network laid over the physical network.
entries.recognitionCue: If the network exists logically across underlying infrastructure → think overlay network.

entries.title: Virtual Machine (VM) Networks
paragraphs: A virtual machine network provides network connectivity for virtual machines.
Virtual machines need virtual networking to communicate with other virtual machines, hosts, external networks, and other services.
Think: The network where the virtual machines communicate.
entries.recognitionCue: If the scenario is about basic network connectivity for virtual machines → think VM network.

entries.title: Local Storage
paragraphs: Local storage resides directly on or within the virtualization host.
The advantage is simplicity and direct access. The major consideration is that the storage is tied more closely to that particular host.
Think: The disk lives with the host.
entries.recognitionCue: If virtual machine storage exists directly on its virtualization host → think local storage.

entries.title: Storage Area Network (SAN)
paragraphs: A storage area network provides networked block storage.
Servers can access storage across a storage network while treating that storage more like disk volumes.
Think: Shared network storage presented as blocks.
entries.recognitionCue: If multiple systems need network-based block storage → think SAN.

entries.title: Network-Attached Storage (NAS)
paragraphs: Network-attached storage provides network-accessible file storage.
Systems access shared files and directories over a network.
Think: Shared files across the network.
entries.recognitionCue: If multiple systems need shared network files → think NAS.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Independent virtualization host → Stand-alone
Hosts operate together → Clustering
Duplicate an existing virtual machine → Cloning
Virtual machine should run on a specified host → Host affinity
Virtual machine needs direct physical device access → Hardware pass-through
Virtual network built over underlying infrastructure → Overlay network
Network connectivity for virtual machines → VM network
Disk attached to host → Local storage
Shared network block storage → SAN
Shared network file storage → NAS

entries.title: Cloning vs. Clustering
paragraphs: Cloning copies a virtual machine. Clustering groups hosts or resources together.

entries.title: SAN vs. NAS
paragraphs: This is the major recognition distinction: SAN means block storage; NAS means file storage.

entries.title: Host Affinity vs. Hardware Pass-Through
paragraphs: Host affinity controls where the virtual machine runs. Hardware pass-through controls which physical device the virtual machine accesses directly.
